author: Eustathius of Antioch
occasion: Eustathius responds to a philosopher's questions about the creation of animals and humanity in Genesis, defending the distinct creation of humanity in God's image and likeness and the co-creative role of the Son.
argument: Eustathius argues that the animals and birds formed from the earth in Genesis 2 are distinct from those created earlier from the waters, since only these are said to be 'formed' by God's own hand. He notes that these earth-formed creatures may be interpreted as the nations gathered into the Church, though he also offers a literal reading. He contends that humanity's being made a second ruler over all the earth is what it means to be made according to God's image and likeness. He then addresses the plural 'let us make' in Genesis 1:26, arguing that it introduces a co-creating person. Since the Father who speaks and the one addressed are both God, the phrase reveals the shared deity of the Father and the Son, and Eustathius concludes by identifying the Son as the simple, uncompounded image of God.

outline.move: Eustathius distinguishes the earth-formed animals and birds of Genesis 2 from the earlier water-born creatures, noting that only these are said to be 'formed' by God's own hand rather than by command.

He argues that these newly formed beasts and birds may represent the nations gathered into the Church, while also offering a literal reading, and he identifies humanity's rule over the earth as the meaning of being made in God's image and likeness.
He raises the question of whom God addressed when saying 'let us make humanity,' pressing the philosopher to consider the plural form.
He concludes that the plural 'let us make' reveals a co-creating person, that the Father and the Son share one deity, and that the Son is the simple, uncompounded image of God.

cast.name: Eustathius of Antioch
cast.who: The author, bishop of Antioch, writing in defense of the Church's reading of Genesis; he speaks in the first person but is not named in the surviving fragments.

cast.name: the philosopher
cast.who: An unnamed interlocutor whose questions Eustathius is answering.

voices.speaker: God (quoted from Genesis)
voices.how_marked: Introduced by phrases such as 'by saying' and 'he said'

scripture: The author quotes Genesis in a form close to the Septuagint. Citations should use modern English conventions: Genesis 1:26-27 and Genesis 2 for the creation of animals and humanity. Psalm numbering follows the Septuagint where applicable.
uncertain: The exact date of the work is unknown.
The identity of the philosopher addressed is not stated in the surviving fragments.
The precise extent of the original treatise cannot be determined from the fragments.
Whether Eustathius ultimately prefers the allegorical reading of the beasts as nations or the literal reading cannot be determined from the surviving text.

_unresolved_facts.claim: He notes that these earth-formed creatures may be interpreted as the nations gathered into the Church, though he also offers a literal reading.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ἔστιν εἰπεῖν ὅτι ἔθνη εἰσὶ ταῦτα τὰ θηρία τὰ ἐν τῇ Ἐκκλησίᾳ ὑπὸ Θεοῦ συναχθέντα ἢ ὅτι ἱππὼν καὶ συβόσιον καὶ καμηλοστάσιον καὶ οἰοτρόφυον (...) σήμερον ὁ παράδεισος ὑπάρχει. Οὐχ οὕτως, ὦ φιλόσοφε
_unresolved_facts.fix: Eustathius presents the allegorical reading (beasts as nations gathered into the Church) but immediately rejects it with 'Οὐχ οὕτως, ὦ φιλόσοφε' ('Not so, philosopher'), insisting instead on a literal reading of the animals as horse, swine, camel, and sheep stock.

_unresolved_facts.claim: He contends that humanity's being made a second ruler over all the earth is what it means to be made according to God's image and likeness.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: τοῦτο τὸ κύριόν ἐστι τοῦ ποιῆσαι τὸν ἄνθρωπον κατ' εἰκόνα Θεοῦ καὶ ἄρχειν αὐτὸν πάσης τῆς γῆς
_unresolved_facts.fix: Eustathius states that humanity's rule over the earth is the purpose (τὸ κύριόν ἐστι τοῦ ποιῆσαι) for which humanity was made according to God's image, not that being a 'second ruler' is itself the meaning of 'image and likeness.' The 'second ruler' language (δεύτερον ἄρχοντα) appears in u01-rem-mid as a description, not a definition of the image.

_unresolved_facts.claim: and Eustathius concludes by identifying the Son as the simple, uncompounded image of God
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ἡ γὰρ τοῦ Θεοῦ εἰκὼν ἁπλῆ καὶ ἀσύνθετός ἐστι, πῦρ οὖσα τῇ φύσει
_unresolved_facts.fix: The text states 'the image of God is simple and uncompounded, being fire by nature' (ἡ γὰρ τοῦ Θεοῦ εἰκὼν), but does not explicitly identify 'the Son' as this image in the surviving text. The antecedent of 'the image of God' is grammatically ambiguous—it could refer to the Son, but the text does not explicitly say 'the Son is the image.' The brief overstates the identification.

_unresolved_facts.claim: while also offering a literal reading
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Οὐχ οὕτως, ὦ φιλόσοφε, ἀλλ' ἢ τὸ εἰπεῖν τὸν Θεόν
_unresolved_facts.fix: Eustathius rejects the allegorical reading and insists on the literal reading; he does not 'also offer' a literal reading as an alternative option.

_unresolved_facts.claim: and he identifies humanity's rule over the earth as the meaning of being made in God's image and likeness
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: τοῦτο τὸ κύριόν ἐστι τοῦ ποιῆσαι τὸν ἄνθρωπον κατ' εἰκόνα Θεοῦ καὶ ἄρχειν αὐτὸν πάσης τῆς γῆς
_unresolved_facts.fix: Eustathius presents humanity's rule as the purpose for which humanity was made in God's image, not as the definition or meaning of 'image and likeness' itself.

_unresolved_facts.claim: he speaks in the first person
_unresolved_facts.fix: Eustathius does not use the first person in the surviving fragments; he speaks in the third person or addresses the philosopher directly using second person ('ζητήσωμεν, φιλόσοφε').
